The bug comes from the `ordering_parts` regex on `SQLCompiler`. Without `re.DOTALL`, `.` doesn't match newlines, so on multiline RawSQL the search only matched the last line that contains ASC/DESC. `get_order_by()` then used that last line in its `seen` duplicate check, so different clauses with identical last lines looked like duplicates. The code here already has the fix: the pattern is `r"^(.*)\s(?:ASC|DESC).*"` compiled with `re.MULTILINE | re.DOTALL`, so the match covers the whole multiline SQL. `get_order_by()` uses it at compiler.py:501 (`without_ordering = self.ordering_parts.search(sql)[1]`). In `_multi_decorate`, `bound_method` is built as `wraps(method)(partial(method.__get__(self, type(self))))`. `wraps(method)` copies `__name__`, `__module__` and the other wrapper assignments onto the partial object. The decorator therefore receives an object that has them, so `func.__name__` no longer raises `AttributeError`.

The fix is already in `AdminReadonlyField.get_admin_url` in `django/contrib/admin/helpers.py`. It now calls `reverse(url_name, args=[quote(remote_obj.pk)], current_app=self.model_admin.admin_site.name)`. This is the same change the report proposed, so the link uses the custom admin site's name instead of defaulting to `/admin/`. I read the code but did not run the tests.
ModelChoiceIteratorValue now defines __hash__ returning hash(self.value), which makes it hashable. The class is in django/forms/models.py.

The crash comes from `Expressions.rename_table_references` in `django/db/backends/ddl_references.py`. During the SQLite table remake the unique index SQL is built with `alias_cols=False`, so its columns carry no table alias. `rename_table_references` runs on the new table name and calls `self.expressions.relabeled_clone({old_table: new_table})`. That gives the columns a table alias, so the index SQL is rendered as `"table"."column"`. SQLite rejects the `.` operator in index expressions, which is the error in the traceback.

I haven't run this or applied a fix. The likely fix is to set `col.alias = new_table` on the columns of a deep copy of the expressions instead of relabelling. This is from my memory of the upstream Django change, and I didn't check it against this repo.

The fix belongs in RenameModel.database_forwards in corpus/django/db/migrations/operations/models.py. It currently calls schema_editor.alter_db_table and then alters related fields without checking whether the table name changed. Add `old_db_table = old_model._meta.db_table` and `new_db_table = new_model._meta.db_table` after the `old_model` lookup. Then add `if old_db_table == new_db_table: return` before the alter_db_table call. When db_table is already set, the rename then does nothing: Postgres keeps its foreign key constraints and SQLite doesn't recreate the table. I haven't made or run this change.

MultiWidget.id_for_label in corpus/django/forms/widgets.py (line 937) is the method the issue is about. The provided `URLValidator.__call__` in `django/core/validators.py` already wraps `urlsplit(value)` in a `try/except ValueError` that re-raises as `ValidationError`, so this version should not leak the `ValueError`. The fix is in `NegatedExpression.as_sql`. `~Q(pk__in=[])` becomes a `NegatedExpression`, and compiling an empty `pk__in` raises `EmptyResultSet`. The method catches it and returns the always-true expression. That is `1=1` on backends that don't support boolean expressions in SELECT, and `Value(True)` otherwise. Before this handling, the exception left an empty SELECT column, which gave `SELECT AS "foo"`.

MigrationRecorder.ensure_schema (django/db/migrations/recorder.py) creates the django_migrations table via editor.create_model(self.Migration) without consulting router.allow_migrate; record_applied/record_unapplied call it unconditionally, and applied_migrations/has_table also ignore the router.

The fix is already in the Subquery constructor, which sets `self.query.subquery = True` on its cloned query. Because of that, `Query.as_sql()` wraps the SQL in parentheses. The `subquery_sql[1:-1]` slice in `Subquery.as_sql()` then removes those parentheses instead of the first and last characters of the SQL.

The fix is in MessageEncoder.default in cookie.py. It now checks `if obj.extra_tags is not None:` instead of testing truthiness. An empty-string extra_tags is therefore appended to the encoded message and survives a round trip.

The template autoreload `file_changed` handler, `template_changed`, causes this. When BASE_DIR is in `DIRS`, every project file sits under a template directory. The handler resets the template loaders and returns True, which tells the autoreloader the change was handled, so it skips the restart. The check on line 49 (`if file_path.suffix == ".py": return`) makes the handler ignore Python files so they still trigger a restart. This copy of the code already has that check. I read the file but didn't run the repro.

The bug is in RenameIndex.database_backwards(). When old_fields is set (an unnamed index), it returns early as a no-op (comment: "Backward operation with unnamed index is a no-op."). The auto-generated name is never restored, so re-applying forwards tries to rename to a name that already exists.

BaseCommand.create_parser (corpus/django/core/management/base.py) sets the parser's help formatter with `kwargs.setdefault("formatter_class", DjangoHelpFormatter)`. A `formatter_class` passed to `create_parser` replaces the default `DjangoHelpFormatter`. The `help` text is passed as `description=self.help`. The default formatter reflows that text, which is why the newlines and indentation in the example were lost. A command can subclass `BaseCommand` and override `create_parser` to pass `formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter`, or a subclass of it, to keep the help layout. I read this code but did not run it.

The code already has this: `django.utils.html.json_script` takes `encoder=None` and calls `json.dumps(value, cls=encoder or DjangoJSONEncoder)`, so callers can pass a custom encoder class. The template filter in `defaultfilters.py` still doesn't expose the parameter, and the code says nothing about documenting `json_script`.

check_for_template_tags_with_the_same_name merges libraries from TEMPLATES OPTIONS['libraries'] (line 58) and auto-discovered templatetags modules (line 61) into one defaultdict(set) keyed by name. The crash is fixed by resolving the related model to its concrete model before building the select mask, so proxy models use the concrete model's _meta (and pk). In _get_only_select_mask: `related_model = field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model`, then `self._get_only_select_mask(related_model._meta, ...)`. The same change is in _get_defer_select_mask at line 746.

In DatabaseClient.settings_to_cmd_args_env (postgresql/client.py), the extra parameters are added with `args.extend(parameters)` before the dbname is appended (`args += [dbname]`). This puts the psql options ahead of the database name, as the issue asks.

Giving it a fixed `template_name = "django/forms/div.html"` in the class body would avoid the warning. It only renders hidden inputs, so the choice of template makes no visible difference. The issue asks for serialization of combined Enum flags, such as `re.UNICODE | re.IGNORECASE`, which previously became the invalid `re.RegexFlag[None]`. The shown `EnumSerializer` already handles this: for `enum.Flag` values it splits the combined value into its member flags (via `list(self.value)` on Python 3.11+, or `enum._decompose` with `reversed` on older versions) and emits them joined with `" | "`, such as `re.RegexFlag['UNICODE'] | re.RegexFlag['IGNORECASE']`.

BaseFormSet.empty_form builds its kwargs with the user's form_kwargs first (**self.get_form_kwargs(None)) and then sets "empty_permitted": True and "use_required_attribute": False after them. The forced values override any empty_permitted passed in form_kwargs, so the setting is ignored for empty_form. That also avoids the conflict with use_required_attribute that forms.py:110 raises as a ValueError. The code at formsets.py:256-266 already has this fix, so I did not change anything.

The IndexError comes from `if str_number[0] == "-":` in `format()` in django/utils/numberformat.py. When the number is null (None or an empty value), `str_number` is an empty string, so indexing `[0]` raises "string index out of range". The upstream Django fix is to use `str_number.startswith("-")`, or to check `str_number[:1]`, instead of indexing. I didn't make that change or run anything.

The fix is in UserChangeForm.__init__ in django/contrib/auth/forms.py: password.help_text is formatted with f"../../{self.instance.pk}/password/" instead of "../password/", so the link works when the user is reached via to_field.

Model Field.formfield() sets defaults["show_hidden_initial"] = True when the field's default is callable (e.g. ArrayField default=list). This causes the hidden "initial-..." input to be rendered, which leads to the inline being treated as unchanged on resubmission and bypassing validation.
get_latest_lastmod uses max([...], default=None), so an empty items() list returns None instead of raising ValueError.

The `has_key` in the corpus no longer has the reported race. It drops the `os.path.exists()` pre-check, opens the file directly, and returns `False` on `FileNotFoundError`, so a file deleted by another thread (including by `_is_expired`) is handled instead of raising. This matches the ranked match at `filebased.py:91`, but I'm inferring from that match rather than from a direct view of the method's full current source.

create_permissions looked up ContentTypes without the migrate database, so the router's db_for_read ran. Line 79 in this checkout already has the fix. It uses `ContentType.objects.db_manager(using).get_for_model(klass, for_concrete_model=False)`, so the lookup uses the `using` database passed to the command. In `get_related_selections` (corpus/django/db/models/sql/compiler.py), a FilteredRelation's `local_setter` caches the object as the reverse relation on the parent object. It should only do that when the filtered relation is a single join away from the base model. A multi-level path like `pool__tournament__pool` needs a no-op setter, because otherwise the wrong object gets cached as `tournament`. The condition `partial(local_setter, final_field) if len(joins) <= 2 else local_setter_noop` is that guard, and it's already in this corpus. I haven't run the test case against it. The ranked results didn't point at this spot, so I found it by searching for the setter functions.

In `submit_row`, `show_save_as_new` is `not is_popup and has_add_permission and change and save_as`. The `has_add_permission` check the report asks for is already in this code. AlterField.reduce already handles a following AlterField on the same field. It returns [operation], so consecutive AlterFields collapse into the last one. The check is the isinstance(operation, (AlterField, RemoveField)) condition in AlterField.reduce.

The check for this case is in `_check_list_display_item` in `corpus/django/contrib/admin/checks.py`. It doesn't extend E108. A reverse foreign key like `choice` is found by `get_field()`, so the E108 branch (`FieldDoesNotExist`, then `AttributeError`) never runs for it. The check that follows rejects it with a separate error, `admin.E109`, "must not be a many-to-many field or a reverse foreign key". The condition that does this is on lines 933-936, and the E109 error is built at lines 937-943. I didn't run anything to confirm it.

CreateModel.reduce in django/db/migrations/operations/models.py already handles this: a RenameIndex with old_fields (the index_together to indexes transition) is folded into the CreateModel. It removes the matching entry from options["index_together"] and adds a models.Index with the new name to options["indexes"]. A squashed migration therefore no longer carries index_together, so the deprecation warning goes away. I read the code but did not run a squash to confirm it.

The `join` filter in django/template/defaultfilters.py (lines 594-604) branches on `autoescape`: when on, it escapes both the joining string and the items with conditional_escape; when off, it does a plain `arg.join(value)`. The fix is this `if autoescape:` / `else: data = arg.join(value)` branch.

In Query._get_only_select_mask, the related model is computed as `field.remote_field.model._meta.concrete_model` for every relation. For a reverse relation (e.g. OneToOneRel) this resolves to the wrong model, so the `only()` mask for the reverse-related model (`secondary__secondary_field_1`) isn't applied and all of its fields are selected. The fix is to use `field.related_model._meta.concrete_model` when `field in opts.related_objects`, and keep `field.remote_field.model` for forward relations. I did not run a query to confirm this.

In `QuerySet._batched_insert()`, the condition `if bulk_return and (on_conflict is None or on_conflict == OnConflict.UPDATE)` keeps `returning_fields=self.model._meta.db_returning_fields` when `update_conflicts` is used. That makes `bulk_create(update_conflicts=True)` return the primary keys on backends that can return rows from a bulk insert. `ignore_conflicts` still drops the returning fields. The branch is in `corpus/django/db/models/query.py`.

The bug is in FunctionTypeSerializer.serialize in django/db/migrations/serializer.py. For a classmethod it builds the path from `klass.__name__`, which drops the outer class for nested classes. That gives `appname.models.Capability.default` instead of `appname.models.Profile.Capability.default`. Using `klass.__qualname__` in place of `klass.__name__` would fix it. I haven't made or tested that change.
